tldr: Instead of using multi-jointed anthropomorphic hands or complex belt mechanisms, the authors developed the "Cartesian Hand," an end-effector that enables grasping and relative motion between object parts using only 7 linear degrees of freedom. It achieves simple, highly precise in-hand manipulation across 35 different tools and containers, including screwdriving, pipetting, and operating pliers.
hero_caption: Overall configuration and kinematic model of the Cartesian Hand. Two independently driven parallel grippers are stacked vertically, with each fingertip translating forward and backward to form an orthogonal linkage mechanism with a total of 7 degrees of freedom.
overview:
When getting robots to handle tools and containers, human-like multi-fingered, articulated hands are mechanically and computationally too complex. Simple parallel grippers, on the other hand, provide little ability to fine-tune grasps or manipulate parts relative to one another once grasped. Everyday tasks such as unscrewing a cap, pulling a syringe plunger, or squeezing pliers typically required a second arm to hold the object's body or an external fixture to push against.

To tackle this, the authors shifted their perspective: since the tools themselves already constrain degrees of freedom through mechanisms like threads, pivots, or plungers, orthogonal linear motions on the hand side should be sufficient. The resulting "Cartesian Hand" is an all-linear, 7-DoF end-effector featuring two vertically stacked parallel grippers, four horizontally translating fingertips, and an axis that adjusts the spacing between the upper and lower grippers. Because every joint is linear and orthogonal, the relationship between fingertip positions and joint displacements remains constant everywhere, eliminating singularities and complex nonlinear inverse kinematics.

In evaluations across 35 objects spanning laboratory instruments, manufacturing tools, and household items, the hand performed cap opening/closing, syringe aspiration, pipetting, opening/closing scissors and pliers, and trigger actuation. It achieved a 100% success rate across 10 trials per object (350 trials total). Furthermore, when mounted on both arms of a humanoid robot, two Cartesian Hands coordinated to open a tube cap and dispense liquid with a pipette. This clearly demonstrates that advanced in-hand manipulation can emerge from well-chosen linear motions without having to mimic articulated human fingers.
contributions: Developed the "Cartesian Hand," a 7-DoF end-effector built entirely with linear joints by combining two vertically stacked parallel grippers, four independently translating fingertips, and a vertical gap-adjustment stage.
Systematized a set of reusable linear motion primitives without complex trajectory optimization, taking advantage of a constant kinematic Jacobian and complete absence of singularities.
Achieved a 100% success rate across 350 in-hand manipulation trials on 35 articulated objects spanning laboratory, manufacturing, and household domains.
Transferred the identical hardware and motion primitives directly from a fixed-base robot arm (Franka) to a humanoid robot, demonstrating bimanual cooperative laboratory manipulation.

sections.heading: Why Linear Motion Instead of Articulated Hands?
sections.summary: To handle tools designed for humans, robots need relative motion between grasped parts. Articulated hands are hard to control, and parallel grippers struggle to manipulate objects on their own. This paper introduces the Cartesian Hand, which uses just 7 linear joints to provide independent grasping at two points and relative motion, enabling versatile in-hand manipulation through simple straight-line primitives by leveraging the object's own geometric constraints.
sections.details:
When robots deploy into human environments, simple pick-and-place is not enough. Tasks like unscrewing a bottle cap, drawing liquid with a syringe, or squeezing pliers require grasping an object securely while moving its constituent parts relative to each other.

Historically, two main approaches have addressed this challenge. First are multi-fingered, articulated hands that mimic human hands. While dexterous, their kinematics depend heavily on current pose, and coordinating multi-finger contacts makes learning and control extremely difficult. Second are enhanced grippers with active belts or rollers embedded in the fingertips. While effective for reorienting a single object, they are poorly suited for grasping two separate parts and driving relative motion between them. As a result, operating such tools usually required a second robot arm to steady the base, or pushing the tool against a fixture or tabletop.

The authors propose a fresh alternative: achieving dual-point independent grasping and relative manipulation using purely translational degrees of freedom. Threaded screws advance linearly as they rotate, syringes translate along an axis, and pliers rotate around a single pivot. In other words, most everyday tools and containers already constrain the relative movement between their parts mechanically. The robot hand therefore does not need to reproduce intricate finger flexing; simple combinations of linear motions are more than enough to operate them.

sections.heading: Lineage of Dexterous Hands and Where Cartesian Hand Fits
sections.summary: Research on dexterous in-hand manipulation falls into articulated multi-fingered hands, grippers with actuated contact surfaces (belts/rollers), and methods leveraging external environmental contacts. The Cartesian Hand maintains passive fingertips while arranging linear axes to provide a unique advantage: dual-point independent grasping and relative motion within a single hand.
sections.details:
This section clarifies differences from prior work across three main categories:

- Multi-fingered Articulated Hands:
Featuring human-like multi-jointed fingers, these hands have recently shown flexible behaviors when paired with imitation learning or large foundation models (such as VLAs). However, their mechanical and control complexity remains high, presenting a major barrier to real-world deployment. The Cartesian Hand deliberately avoids articulated joints, relying exclusively on orthogonal linear axes to fundamentally simplify control.

- Contact-Enhanced Grippers:
Designs like BACH and BOP embed active conveyor belts or rollers in their fingertips to roll and translate grasped objects. While great for in-hand reorientation of single rigid bodies, their contact surfaces are mechanically intricate. In contrast, the Cartesian Hand keeps its fingertip surfaces passive (using friction tape) and moves the fingertip structures themselves.

- Articulated Object Manipulation and Extrinsic Dexterity:
Manipulating articulated tools has often relied on "extrinsic dexterity," using environmental fixtures, gravity, or dual-arm coordination. Because the Cartesian Hand grasps two distinct points of an object independently and generates relative motion directly within the hand, it dramatically reduces the need for external jigs or a second arm.

sections.heading: A 7-DoF All-Linear Mechanism and Its Elegant Kinematics
sections.summary: The hand consists of two stacked parallel grippers (2 DoF for opening/closing), independent sliding fingertips for each gripper (4 DoF), and a vertical distance adjustment stage (1 DoF), totaling 7 linear DoF. Since all joints are prismatic, the Jacobian is constant and free of singularities, enabling complex operations like twisting and plunging by combining simple linear motion primitives.
sections.details:
### Mechanical Design Focused on Linear Motion
The architecture of the Cartesian Hand is remarkably streamlined. At its core are two parallel grippers stacked vertically: a base gripper and an auxiliary gripper.

The 7 degrees of freedom are distributed as follows:
- Lower (base) gripper open/close ($q_0$: y-axis, 52 mm stroke)
- Lower left/right fingertip translation ($q_1, q_2$: x-axis, 65 mm stroke each)
- Inter-gripper vertical distance ($q_3$: z-axis, 52 mm stroke)
- Upper (auxiliary) gripper open/close ($q_4$: y-axis, 52 mm stroke)
- Upper left/right fingertip translation ($q_5, q_6$: x-axis, 65 mm stroke each)

Actuation relies on seven low-cost commercial servomotors (Feetech-3915, stall torque 1.39 N·m), converted to linear motion via rack-and-pinion drives and dovetail slides. The fingertips deliver a theoretical push/pull force of up to ~170 N, and a single gripper easily supports a 2 kg bottle. The device weighs 850 g with compact closed dimensions of $166 \times 100 \times 76$ mm. It can be easily fabricated on a 3D printer (PLA or nylon SLS), costs roughly $500 in total components including servos and microcontrollers, and takes about two hours to assemble once printed.

### Pose-Independent Kinematics
What sets this hand apart from articulated hands is its kinematics. Letting $\mathbf{q} \in \mathbb{R}^7$ be the joint displacement vector and $\mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^{12}$ the stacked 3D positions of the four fingertip reference points, their relation is a simple linear map: $\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{J}\mathbf{q}$. Remarkably, the Jacobian matrix $\mathbf{J} \in \mathbb{R}^{12 \times 7}$ is completely constant across the entire workspace. It never changes with joint positions or hand opening. It maintains full column rank ($\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{J}) = 7$) everywhere, so there is zero risk of encountering kinematic singularities. Each fingertip's reachable workspace forms a clean, axis-aligned cuboid.

### Systematizing Motion Primitives
Allowing each of the 7 joints to be either stationary or moving yields $2^7 = 128$ combinations, but accounting for bilateral symmetry and coordination condenses them into just 5 fundamental and 6 composite primitives (11 total). For instance, translating opposing fingertips in reverse directions creates a "twist" that rotates objects held between them. Clamping the body with the lower gripper while moving the upper gripper vertically creates a "plunge / pull" motion. Rotations exceeding the 65 mm fingertip stroke can continue indefinitely by repeating a cycle: clamp and twist $\to$ release and reset $\to$ reclamp and twist.

sections.heading: No Cameras Needed: Contact Detection and Modular Procedures
sections.summary: The hand operates without external visual feedback, automatically estimating object dimensions through proprioceptive contact detection based on servo current limits and velocity drops. By adjusting just a few geometric parameters, the same sequence of motion primitives transfers instantaneously across diverse objects.
sections.details:
### Contact Detection via Joint Control
Operating the Cartesian Hand requires no expensive force sensors or camera feedback. Contacts are detected purely through the servomotors' own position, velocity, and load information (proprioception).

Specifically, a joint moves under a preset torque limit; if its velocity drops below a threshold for a set duration before reaching the target position, it registers as contact. This mechanism proves remarkably practical. When grasping a cap, for example, simply closing the gripper until contact automatically measures the cap's outer diameter. Once the diameter is known, the hand computes on the fly how many millimeters the fingertips must slide and how many regrasp cycles are required to achieve the desired rotation angle.

### Reusable Manipulation Sequences
Tasks are formulated as sequences of pre-defined motion primitives. Objects sharing the same functional mechanism can use the exact same primitive sequence:
- Threaded objects: grasp $\to$ twist $\to$ release $\to$ reset slide $\to$ regrasp cycle
- Syringes and pipettes: lower gripper holds barrel $\to$ upper gripper holds plunger and translates vertically
- Trigger mechanisms (sprayers): gripper opening/closing itself directly pulls the trigger

Adapting to a new object requires no mechanical modifications or control rewrites—only minor parameter tuning such as grasp heights and stroke limits. In experiments, once a sequence was authored for a representative object in a category, a new unseen object required at most five calibration trials to establish working parameters.

sections.heading: Flawless Performance on 35 Objects and Bimanual Humanoid Tasks
sections.summary: Mounted on a Franka arm, the hand completed 10 trials across each of 35 laboratory, manufacturing, and household objects (350 trials total) with a 100% success rate. Mounted on both arms of a humanoid robot, it also successfully executed a fully autonomous bimanual lab protocol, uncapping a tube with one hand while operating a pipette with the other.
sections.details:
### Experimental Setup (V-A)
The evaluation covered 35 distinct objects grouped into three categories:
- Laboratory instruments: 20 mL and 60 mL syringes, micropipette, multichannel pipette, 96-well plate, petri dish, reagent bottles, centrifuge tubes, etc.
- Workshop and manufacturing tools: blowtorch, manual screwdriver, electric screwdriver, scissors, four different pliers, power drill, etc.
- Household items: chopsticks, spray bottle, peanut butter jar, childproof medicine bottle, lightbulb, nasal spray, glue stick, etc.

The hand was first mounted on a Franka Emika Panda arm. Once the object was lifted from the stand, the arm stayed stationary while all in-hand manipulation was performed solely by the Cartesian Hand's linear joints. Ten trials were conducted per object, totaling 350 trials.

### Broad Versatility and Reliability (V-B, V-C)
The results were remarkable: all 350 trials succeeded without a single drop or mid-task failure (100% success rate). Low backlash from the linear sliders, singularity-free deterministic kinematics, and proprioceptive contact adaptation ensured exceptional repeatability.

In a continuous demonstration, a single hand performed three distinct sequential tasks on different tools: pulling a spray trigger, twisting a pipette dial to set volume and plunging it, and twisting open a threaded bottle cap. Seamlessly executing rotations, plunging, and squeezing with purely linear motions showed the power of the concept.

### Humanoid Deployment and Bimanual Coordination (V-D)
Next, Cartesian Hands were mounted on both arms of the Duke Humanoid V2. Beyond modifying arm approach trajectories for the humanoid, the internal hand manipulation routines and parameters remained identical to those used on the Franka arm.

The bimanual benchmark demonstrated an automated laboratory protocol. The left Cartesian Hand held a 50 mL centrifuge tube, using its lower gripper to hold the tube body and its upper gripper to unscrew the cap. Simultaneously, the right Cartesian Hand grasped a micropipette and depressed its plunger, inserting the tip into the opened tube to dispense liquid. Crucially, neither arm had to act as an external holding fixture for the other. Because each hand completed grasp-and-manipulate cycles internally, the arm degrees of freedom were used strictly for spatial positioning.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Outlook: The Value of Deliberate Simplicity
sections.summary: The Cartesian Hand is an innovative end-effector that delivers in-hand manipulation and relative motion using purely linear joints. While currently tailored to internally articulated objects with known initial poses, integrating tactile and visual feedback will expand its autonomy and versatility.
sections.details:
### Summary of Contributions
This work presents a compelling counterargument in robotic manipulation: achieving dexterity does not strictly require complex, multi-jointed human-like hands. By exploiting the mechanical constraints inherent to human tools, a dual-point linear grasp mechanism capable of relative motion delivers surprisingly rich and practical in-hand dexterity.

### Limitations and Next Steps
Several current constraints remain:
- Dependence on Structured Objects:
The design excels on objects whose relative motions are mechanically guided by threads, pistons, slides, or pivots. It is not intended for unconstrained, free-form in-hand reorientation of arbitrary rigid shapes.
- Absence of Visual and High-Precision Tactile Feedback:
Experiments assumed known initial pickup poses on the table without closed-loop visual correction (AprilTags were placed on the hand but unused here). The hand also lacks high-resolution tactile sensors for direct contact force measurement.

Future work will explore integrating tactile sensing arrays on the fingertips to detect slip, as well as closed-loop visual servoing to eliminate manual calibration trials and achieve fully autonomous tool manipulation.

takeaways: Rather than copying articulated human hands, embedding dual-point linear grasping and relative motion directly into an end-effector produces remarkably versatile in-hand manipulation.
An orthogonal linear joint architecture keeps the Jacobian constant across the entire workspace, eliminating singularities and inverse-kinematics failures to deliver deterministic reliability.
Proprioceptive contact sensing via servomotor load variations is sufficient to measure object dimensions and dynamically compute regrasp cycles without external sensors.
When an end-effector can independently handle internal relative motions, bimanual setups are freed from using one arm merely as a passive holding fixture.
limitations: Specialized for articulated objects with mechanically constrained relative motions (threads, pivots, linear guides); unsuitable for dexterous reorientation of arbitrary unconstrained objects.
Lacks real-time closed-loop control from cameras or high-precision force sensors, requiring pre-defined grasp locations and up to five initial calibration trials per new object.
Relies on friction-driven fingertip twisting, which risks slipping on very slick materials or when high torques are required for heavy bolt fastening.
